translation:
The essence of devotion that exists in this world is loving, and it pervades everywhere; this is Kabirji's own quality. Even in the sharpness of his words there is love and compassion for people. And the soul dwelling within the body is a portion separated from Parbrahma; therefore it has been called of the nature of Raghupati (Lord Ram). Because of Kabirji's influence, the deceitful goings-on that were current in Kashi slowed down, and an atmosphere of devotion spread everywhere.

The form of Parbrahma that the scriptures and Puranas describe under the Name "Ram" has, in this Kali Yuga, manifested in the form of Kabir. That is why, for remembrance of the Name in worship, the name "Ramkabir" has been given.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad speaks, in connection with the gods, of one who is "nirvasik" -- meaning one who, while dwelling in a place of shelter, drives away craving. The gods dwell dependent on human beings, living off what is given to them without earning it. One who, while dwelling in such shelter, drives away craving and worships only Parbrahma -- that one alone is a Harijan (a person of Hari). Such are those who give up every hope and craving and worship only the one Parbrahma, who do not even wish for heaven or hell.

Saints and holy ones (sadhu-sant) are always pure and unique; the influence of their love spreads to the four corners of the world. Naturally everyone longs for the darshan of such a saint, but even the darshan of their servants (das) is a matter of great fortune -- so much so that even Vaikunth desires the darshan of such servants.

Even Vaikunth longs for the darshan of a saint, and the Lord of Lakshmi Himself holds the very same longing -- so what then to say of poor, helpless Vaikunth? Jasvantji has told, in his kirtan (hymn), what this Kamalakanth Parbrahma (the Lord of Kamala, i.e. Vishnu) desires.

_Hamaro das basat hai jaanhi |_
_Lakshman sahit sameep Janki | me joon basatahun taanhi ||1||_
_Jab mero keval jan sove tab nikat nisa me jaagu ||_
_Jab mero jan uth chale | tab dor dor sang laagu ||2||_
_Jab mero jan uvate chale | tab kar grahi baat bataau ||_
_Apne pitambar-ki karu chhaanh | ham jab tab sang rahun ||3||_
_Mope ber kare me sahun | mere jan-ku sahyo nav jaai ||_
_Bal bal vaani shri mukh keri | jan Jasvante gaai ||4||_

(Wherever My devotee dwells, there I remain, together with Lakshman and Janki nearby. ||1|| When My true devotee is asleep, I stay awake close by him in the night; when he rises and sets out, I run along close beside him. ||2|| When My devotee strays from the path, I take his hand and show him the way; I hold the shade of My own yellow garment over him -- I remain with him at all times. ||3|| If someone bears enmity toward Me, I bear with it, but I cannot bear anyone wronging My devotee. Blessed, blessed is this speech from the Lord's own mouth, sung by devotee Jasvant. ||4||)

This is Jasvantji's testimony (sakhi) verse. Parbrahma says: wherever My devotee dwells, there I remain together with Lakshman and Sitaji; when he falls asleep, I stay awake near him; when he rises and sets about his work, I remain with him; and if he goes astray or does something wrong, I show him the way as well. And if someone bears enmity toward Me, I bear it, but I cannot bear any offense against My devotee. It is for this very reason that Parbrahma has been called Bhaktavatsal, one who loves his devotees dearly. This verse was sung by Jasvantji, and Jaydevji bears witness to it -- a saying from the Ashtapadi Gita Govinda.

_Patati patre vichalati patre shankita bhavad-upayaanam |_
_Rachayati shayanam sachakita-nayanam pashyati tava panthaanam ||_
_Dheer sameere Yamuna-teere vasati vane Vanamaali ||29||_
(Gita Govinda 5-11-3)

(When a leaf falls, when a leaf stirs, she suspects it is Your arrival; with startled eyes she prepares the bed and watches for Your path. By the calm-breezed banks of the Yamuna, Vanamali dwells in the grove.)

Purport (bhavarth): Shri Krishna, for the joy of union, has gone to the trysting place; His beauty is supreme, like that of ten million Kandarps (Cupids). Such is Shri Krishna, seated on the banks of the Yamuna, where a gentle, fragrant breeze is blowing.

Made eager at the very hint of Radha's name, He plays the flute in a sweet tone; He even loves the dust flying on the breeze that has touched your (Radha's) body. Krishna, so eager for Radha's arrival, watches your path on every side -- if a bird stirs on one side, or leaves fall from the trees, Krishna looks all around for your path, and prepares a bed of leaves for you. Just as eagerly as Shri Krishna waits for Radha, with that same eagerness the Lord remains eager to look after His devotee, wherever he may dwell. Finally...

In the Mahabharata there is an episode: once Durvasa, together with his community of disciples, became a guest of Duryodhan. After enjoying full hospitality there, when the pleased Durvasa told the king to ask for whatever boon he desired, Duryodhan -- seeing that everything had gone exactly according to plan -- said to the sage, as pre-arranged: just as you are pleased with me, show that same grace to my elder brother Yudhishthir also, and go to him at an inopportune time to receive his hospitality.

Duryodhan began to feel pleased at the thought that the Pandavas, living in poverty in the forest, would fail to honor the sage properly and would thus be cursed by Durvasa, and his own purpose would be accomplished. Hearing Duryodhan's words, Durvasa set out at once to meet the Pandavas; arriving at an inopportune time, he expressed a wish for a meal, and came to the riverbank together with his community of disciples to bathe.

Meanwhile Draupadi grew greatly distressed -- there was not a single grain of food left in the house -- and what if the sage were not pleased? What a disaster that would be! In this distress, Draupadi remembered Krishna, her companion in times of crisis. Hearing his sister's call, Krishna arrived at once. Learning of her distress, through His unfailing power He easily took away the hunger of Durvasa and his whole community of disciples, and they began to feel fully satisfied -- so much so that everyone felt not a single grain of food could enter their stomachs any longer. Durvasa began to lament that he had made Draupadi cook food for nothing; since no more food could now be eaten, her cooking would go to waste -- and if that happened, the Pandavas would burn them to ashes.

_Vritha paakena raajarsher-aparaadh: kritoo mahaan ||_
_Maa smaana-dhaakshur drishtaiva Paandavaah kroor-chakshushaa ||21||_
_Smritvaanu-bhaavam raajarsher-Ambarishasya dheemata: ||_
_Bibhemi sutaraam vipraa Hari-paadaashrayaaj-janaat ||22||_
_Kruddhaas-te nirdaheyur-vai toola-raashim-ivaanala: ||_
_Tata etaan prishtvaiva shishyaah shighram palaayata ||23||_

(Truly, by having food cooked needlessly, without hunger, we have committed a great offense against the royal sage Yudhishthir. Let it not happen that the Pandavas turn a fierce gaze on us and burn us to ashes! O brahmins, remembering the power of the supremely wise King Ambarish, I remain truly afraid of such devotees as have taken refuge at the feet of Lord Hari. If the Pandavas grow angry, they can burn us to ashes in the same way fire burns a heap of hay. So, O disciples, let us flee from here at once, without even asking the Pandavas.)

Truly, by having food cooked needlessly (without hunger), we have committed a great offense against the royal sage Yudhishthir; let it not happen that the Pandavas look on us with a fierce gaze and burn us to ashes! O brahmins, remembering the power of the supremely wise King Ambarish, I truly remain afraid of such devotees, who have taken refuge at the feet of Lord Shri Hari. If the Pandavas fall into anger, they can burn us to ashes in that very way -- as one might set fire to a heap of hay. So, O disciples, let us flee from here at once, without even asking the Pandavas.

In this way Durvasa, having grown frightened, left from there without meeting the Pandavas. Sahadev wandered far and wide searching for him, but could find no trace of him anywhere, until some ascetics related to him the account as told above. Then Krishna, consoling the Pandavas, says --

_Dharma-nityaastu ye kechin-na te seedanti karhichit ||24||_

(Those who are ever devoted to dharma, who remain righteous, never fall into distress.)

Looking at this chapter as a whole, Jivanji Maharaj has drawn our attention to many matters, and has also expounded some points at length. If we look at the main subject, it is this: "Morli Manohar Parmeshwar te khara" (He alone is truly the flute-charming Supreme Lord). On this subject Jivanji Maharaj has, in a very simple way, clearly stated whom to worship, how to worship, and whom to accept as Parbrahma, and why. Here he has shown the true identity of Parbrahma, and has also shown the unity of form between Ram and Krishna. At the same time, he has brought together Akar (form) and Nirakar (formlessness). This matter of Akar-Nirakar had already been discussed earlier in a separate chapter, but here it has been explained again, still more clearly. And he has given the clear instruction that, rising above the debates that go on over Sagun and Nirgun, we should recognize and worship our own Parmeshwar.

The second important point is avatarvad, the doctrine of incarnation. On this question Jivanji Maharaj's stance is entirely clear. Without being drawn by worldly thinking, and remaining above worldly or material desire, he speaks only of devotion to Parmeshwar -- and that too, pure devotion free of any expectation or aspiration, and free of any kind of bondage. He has also, indirectly, indicated in this chapter that devotees of God should not fall into any false debates, for the bond among devotees is one of love. Devotees are bound by the thread of love, not of argument; there can never be any difference of opinion among devotees -- devotees are joined heart to heart through feeling and love. He has shown this point in particular through the example of Rankaji and Vankaji. This is a beautiful illustration of what kind of thread of devotion should exist between two differing positions. Further, staying apart from the many avatars, gods and goddesses, and the various paths, mantras and vows of worship, and instead worshipping the one Parbrahma alone with pure body and mind, living the same simple life as the devotees who have gone before in this world -- this is how the task entrusted by God is to be carried through. On this point too Jivanji Maharaj has left no room for lengthy debate; he has further endorsed it through Kabirji's sakhis, explaining it in a still simpler way. The devotees of Jivanji Maharaj now have only to follow accordingly.

The third point -- small, but important -- is nitya-sada vasant, the ever-present, eternal spring. In very few words Jivanji Maharaj has said a great deal here. Vasant (spring) means joy and celebration, the exchange of love; for devotees, the season of shishir -- that is, autumn's decline -- never comes; it is ever joy and only joy, because there is no obstacle on the path of devotion; here there is no need for scriptural knowledge or great scholarship. A devotee may be without even literacy, while a learned pandit remains weighed down under the burden of his own knowledge, entangled in the web of the scriptures. The knowledgeable one must keep changing his knowledge with each season; and further, just as a sword must be kept clean so that it does not rust, knowledge too must be kept sharp -- whereas devotion gathers no such rust at all. Vasant is the symbol of devotion; it is also the very best time for worship (upasana).

With the example of King Ambarish, Jivanji Maharaj proves Parbrahma's tender love for his devotees. Devotees should worship Shri Hari without any fear. Parbrahma is always ready to protect his devotees -- this we have already seen earlier, so there is no need to speak of it again here.

Finally, Jivanji Maharaj speaks of the oneness between Kabirji and Parbrahma. Their two names are different, their forms are different, yet there is no difference at all between the two -- here he has spoken of this "difference that is without difference." He has shown Kabirji's identity with Parbrahma, presenting here the union of the soul with Parbrahma. In the end, he brings this to completion by showing the unbroken bond between Shri Krishna and Radhika -- she who has stolen his mind, whom he searches for restlessly, his eyes startled, looking about him on every side in doubt for her. Finally, let us take in one sakhi of Kabirji.

_Man mera nirmal bhaya | jaise chokha nir ||_
_Pichhe pichhe Hari phirat | kahat Kabir Kabir ||58||_

(My mind has become pure, like clear water; behind me, behind me, Hari wanders, calling out "Kabir, Kabir.")

That is, Kabirji says: I do not go about following behind God -- rather, God goes about behind me, calling out my own name, "Kabir, Kabir."

That is to say: for one whose mind has become wholly devoted to God, nothing like a separate self or a separate world remains any longer -- and God Himself takes care of such devotees of His.
